accepted.question_text: Let ABC be a triangle with centroid G, and let G_A, G_B, and G_C be the orthogonal projections of G onto the sidelines BC, CA, and AB, respectively. Determine whether the concurrence of the cevians AG_A, BG_B, and CG_C forces ABC to be isosceles, and conversely whether isosceles triangles have this concurrence.

evidence.quote: In this note, we provide a proof of the problem in (*), and we place it in a more general context.

accepted.question_text: Let ABC be a triangle. For a point P in the plane of ABC, let P_A, P_B, and P_C be the orthogonal projections of P onto the side lines BC, CA, and AB, respectively, and define P* when the cevians AP_A, BP_B, and CP_C are concurrent. Let R be the Gergonne point, the point of concurrence of the cevians from the vertices to the points where the incircle touches the opposite sides, and let N be the Nagel point, the point of concurrence of the cevians from the vertices to the points where the respective excircles touch the opposite sides. Determine whether R* exists and whether N* exists, and whether in each case existence is equivalent to ABC being isosceles.

evidence.quote: it is natural to wonder whether exists, where is the Gergonne point.
A similar proof applies to the Nagel point.

accepted.question_text: Using the same definition of P* for orthogonal projections from a point P to the sides of a triangle ABC, find proofs of the Gergonne-point and Nagel-point existence criteria that avoid reliance on Maple or computational algebra and are more geometric or elegant.

evidence.quote: would be interesting to come up with proofs that are more elegant, more geometric, and less computational.

accepted.question_text: Let ABC be an isosceles triangle with AB = AC, let AD be the altitude from A, and let H be the orthocenter. For a point P on AD, project P orthogonally to AB and AC, and let P* be the point on AD where the two corresponding cevians from C and B intersect. Starting from P[0] = P and iterating P[n+1] = P[n]*, analyze the modes of convergence in cases not already covered by the monotone acute-triangle case with the starting point below A and outside the exceptional points.

evidence.quote: Examining the modes of convergence in other cases may turn out to be a nice project

accepted.question_text: Let ABC be a triangle and P an interior point. Let P(A), P(B), and P(C) be the intersections of the cevians AP, BP, and CP with the side lines BC, CA, and AB, respectively. Erect perpendiculars to BC, CA, and AB at P(A), P(B), and P(C), and define P(*) when those three perpendiculars are concurrent. For standard triangle centers such as the centroid, circumcenter, incenter, orthocenter, Gergonne point, and Nagel point, determine the analogues for P(*) of the existence and identification questions asked for P*.

evidence.quote: The questions that were asked about can now be asked about , and this may turn out to lead to interesting results.
